I've been working this land for 40 years. I know how it behaves. My main system is wheat in winter, then maize on the same ground in summer — that's 10 mu. The other 3.1 mu I keep in cotton. That's how I've always split it, and it gives me grain for the household and cash from cotton.

Cotton picking gets harder every year at my age, and fewer hands are home now with the young ones working in town. But I won't give up cotton entirely — it pays better than grain when prices are decent.

For wheat, I plough before planting — that's how I've always prepared the field and I'm not changing that. I'll use the improved variety from the county seed station, the one everyone around here uses. Three irrigations: once before sowing, once at jointing, once when the heads are forming. I apply fertilizer in two goes — base before sowing, top dressing at jointing. Two pesticide sprays, one for weeds early on, one for aphids or rust later.

After wheat harvest in June, I go straight into maize with rotary tillage — faster, and I don't have time to plough again. Hybrid seed, that's standard now, no point using anything else for maize. Two irrigations if the summer rains are poor, maybe just one if it rains well. One pesticide application for corn borers.

Cotton gets ploughed in spring. More water, more spraying — that crop needs attention all summer. Five pesticide passes at least, for aphids, bollworm, and mites. Four irrigations spaced through the season.

I won't try anything new this year. What I know has fed nine people for decades.
